transcript.content: Hi, I’m glad you came in today. What brings you in?

I've been hearing voices and seeing things that aren't actually there, and it's really scaring me. This has been happening for almost two years now, probably about a year and eleven months. I just don't know what to do anymore.

During these two years, have you also had times lasting days to weeks when you felt extremely high or energetic, or very depressed? If so, did the voices and visions happen only during those mood episodes or also when your mood felt normal?
No, I haven't really experienced those kinds of extreme mood swings over the past two years. My mood has been relatively normal, even though the voices and visions keep happening.

Over these two years, have the voices and visions caused major problems in your daily life, like work, school, relationships, or taking care of yourself? Or aside from these experiences, have you been functioning pretty normally?

Yes, it has caused a lot of problems, and I've really struggled to keep up with my work and taking care of myself. I also don't really talk to my friends or family anymore because managing all of this has just been too hard.

latest_inference.note: Previously the candidates were ["Schizophrenia", "Delusional Disorder"]. Based on this conversation, Delusional Disorder now seems unlikely because the patient reports prominent hallucinations (hearing voices and seeing things) with marked functional decline in work, self-care, and social relationships over nearly two years. This pattern is more consistent with Schizophrenia. Mood-related disorders with psychosis are less supported because the patient denies sustained manic or depressive episodes and says the psychotic symptoms occur while mood is relatively normal. The current candidate is therefore ["Schizophrenia"].

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient reports persistent hallucinations for nearly two years with significant functional decline in work, self-care, and social relationships. They deny distinct manic or major depressive episodes, making schizoaffective disorder or mood disorders with psychotic features less likely. The chronic psychotic symptoms with marked impairment are most consistent with schizophrenia.
